newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters' Carey says trade next battleground.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters' Carey says trade next battleground.

text.p: Teamsters President Ron Carey said on Tuesday that major trade legislation will be the next battleground for the union now that it has tentatively settled a strike against United Parcel Service.

Carey told a news conference that the union will fight to stop so-called fast track trade legislation that would allow U.S. officials to negotiate an expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) and other trade agreements.

Carey said the two-week strike by 185,000 UPS workers against the nation's largest package delivery service was a battle against a "throw-away workers" approach by corporations. The two sides have reached tentative agreement on a settlement and striking workers are expected to return to their jobs this week.

NAFTA, Carey said, was part of the "same throw-away worker concept. Throw away the jobs of American workers, exploit workers in countries like Mexico for $4 a day and then, if they start to get organized, move from one place to another."

President Clinton is expected to send to Congress proposed trade negotiation legislation next month and launch an all-out campaign to win its passage by the end of the year. Under the so-called fast track legislation, Congress gives up its right to amend trade agreements and agrees to vote only for them or against them.
Labor unions, who view NAFTA as a job loser for American workers, have vowed to fight the proposed fast track legislation.
Administration officials, who argue NAFTA is needed to open markets to more U.S. exports, have said they hope to have new trade negotiation authority in place by the end of the year.

The administration has been without fast track authority since 1994 and an effort to renew it in 1995 failed becuase Republicans, who control Congress, and Democrats could not agree on whether it should include authority to negotiate labor and environmental issues as part of trade agreements.

Republicans oppose including those issues, while some Democrats have said they will not support legislation that does not include them. Administration officials have been working to develop compromise legislation that would win support from both parties.
